claim: Munc13-1 plays a crucial role in neurotransmitter release.
source: Munc13-1 plays a crucial role in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal region of Munc13-1 encompassing the C1, C2B, MUN and C2C domains (C1C2BMUNC2C) bridges the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes through interactions involving the C2C domain and the C1-C2B region.
source: We recently proposed that the C-terminal region encompassing the C1, C2B, MUN and C2C domains of Munc13-1 (C1C2BMUNC2C) bridges the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes through interactions involving the C2C domain and the C1-C2B region.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is tested experimentally throughout the manuscript using cryo-ET, liposome clustering, and fusion assays.

claim: C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes through opposite ends of its elongated structure.
source: Here we show that C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes through opposite ends of its elongated structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-ET images showing elongated densities bridging two liposomes (Figure 3).

claim: Mutations in putative membrane-binding sites of the C2C domain disrupt the ability of C1C2BMUNC2C to bridge liposomes.
source: Mutations in putative membrane-binding sites of the C2C domain disrupt the ability of C1C2BMUNC2C to bridge liposomes and to mediate liposome fusion in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by DLS data showing that mutations like R1598E/F1658E abolish liposome clustering (Figure 5).

claim: Mutations in putative membrane-binding sites of the C2C domain disrupt the ability of C1C2BMUNC2C to mediate liposome fusion in vitro.
source: Mutations in putative membrane-binding sites of the C2C domain disrupt the ability of C1C2BMUNC2C to bridge liposomes and to mediate liposome fusion in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid and content mixing assays showing that mutations like R1598E/F1658E abolish fusion (Figure 6).

claim: Mutations in the C2C domain lead to disruptive effects on synaptic vesicle docking in mouse neurons.
source: These mutations lead to corresponding disruptive effects on synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in mouse neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing reduced numbers of docked vesicles in neurons expressing mutant Munc13-1 (Figure 9).

claim: Mutations in the C2C domain lead to disruptive effects on synaptic vesicle priming in mouse neurons.
source: These mutations lead to corresponding disruptive effects on synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in mouse neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced RRP in neurons expressing mutant Munc13-1 (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Mutations in the C2C domain lead to disruptive effects on Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in mouse neurons.
source: These mutations lead to corresponding disruptive effects on synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in mouse neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced EPSC amplitudes in neurons expressing mutant Munc13-1 (Figures 7, 8).

claim: A single residue substitution (F1658E) in the 200 kDa Munc13-1 protein almost completely abrogates neurotransmitter release.
source: Remarkably, these effects include an almost complete abrogation of release by a single residue substitution in this 200 kDa protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data showing that the F1658E mutation nearly abolishes evoked release (Figure 7E).

claim: Bridging the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes is a central function of Munc13-1.
source: These results show that bridging the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes is a central function of Munc13-1.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation between impaired membrane bridging in vitro and disrupted neurotransmitter release in neurons.

claim: The release of neurotransmitters by Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle exocytosis is crucial for interneuronal communication.
source: The release of neurotransmitters by Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle exocytosis is crucial for interneuronal communication.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, cited as background knowledge.

claim: Exocytosis occurs in several steps including tethering, priming, and Ca2+-triggered fusion.
source: Exocytosis occurs in several steps that include tethering of synaptic vesicles to specialized sites of the presynaptic plasma membrane known as active zones, priming of the vesicles to a release-ready state(s) and Ca2+-triggered fusion of the vesicles with the plasma membrane when an action potential causes Ca2+ influx into the presynaptic terminal (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Südhof, 2013, a review article on the topic.

claim: SNAREs (synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1, and SNAP-25) form a tight four-helix bundle called the SNARE complex that brings vesicle and plasma membranes together and is critical for membrane fusion.
source: Central components of this machinery are the SNAP receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, which form a tight four-helix bundle called the SNARE complex that brings the vesicle and plasma membranes together and is critical for membrane fusion (Hanson et al., 1997; Poirier et al., 1998; Söllner et al., 1993; Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and functional studies of SNAREs.

claim: The SNARE complex is disassembled by NSF and SNAPs.
source: The SNARE complex is disassembled by N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor (NSF) and soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAPs) (Söllner et al., 1993), whereas its assembly is orchestrated in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner by Munc18-1 and Munc13s (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on SNARE complex disassembly and assembly.

claim: SNARE complex assembly is orchestrated in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner by Munc18-1 and Munc13s.
source: The SNARE complex is disassembled by N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor (NSF) and soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAPs) (Söllner et al., 1993), whereas its assembly is orchestrated in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner by Munc18-1 and Munc13s (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2013.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1.
source: The assembly pathway involves binding of Munc18-1 to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and to synaptobrevin to template SNARE complex formation (Baker et al., 2015; Parisotto et al., 2014; Sitarska et al., 2017) with the help of Munc13s, which facilitate opening of syntaxin-1 to form the SNARE complex (Ma et al., 2011; Richmond et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to synaptobrevin to template SNARE complex formation.
source: The assembly pathway involves binding of Munc18-1 to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and to synaptobrevin to template SNARE complex formation (Baker et al., 2015; Parisotto et al., 2014; Sitarska et al., 2017) with the help of Munc13s, which facilitate opening of syntaxin-1 to form the SNARE complex (Ma et al., 2011; Richmond et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical and structural studies.

claim: Munc13s facilitate opening of syntaxin-1 to form the SNARE complex.
source: The assembly pathway involves binding of Munc18-1 to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and to synaptobrevin to template SNARE complex formation (Baker et al., 2015; Parisotto et al., 2014; Sitarska et al., 2017) with the help of Munc13s, which facilitate opening of syntaxin-1 to form the SNARE complex (Ma et al., 2011; Richmond et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 acts as the major Ca2+ sensor that triggers release through interactions with membranes and the SNARE complex.
source: Synaptotagmin-1 acts as the major Ca2+ sensor that triggers release through a combination of interactions with membranes and the SNARE complex (Brewer et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2018; Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on synaptotagmin-1 function.

claim: Mammalian Munc13s and their invertebrate homologues Unc13s are essential for neurotransmitter release.
source: Particularly important is to elucidate the functions of mammalian Munc13s and their invertebrate homologues, Unc13s, because these large (ca. 200 kDa) proteins are essential for release (Richmond et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002) and modulate exocytosis in multiple presynaptic plasticity processes through the various domains in its architecture (Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic knockout studies.

claim: Munc13-1 is the most abundant isoform in the mammalian brain.
source: Munc13-1, the most abundant isoform in the mammalian brain, contains a variable N-terminal region with a C2A domain and a calmodulin-binding region (CaMb), as well as a conserved C-terminal region that includes the C1, C2B, MUN and C2C domains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Munc13-1 expression.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2A domain forms a homodimer and alternatively a heterodimer with RIMs.
source: The C2A domain forms a homodimer and alternatively a heterodimer with the Rab3 effectors called RIMs (Betz et al., 2001; Dulubova et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2006), thus providing a switch that controls neurotransmitter release and couples exocytosis to diverse forms of Rab3- and RIM-dependent presynaptic plasticity (Camacho et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2011; Rizo and Südhof, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: The Munc13-1 CaMb region mediates some forms of Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity.
source: the CaMb region mediates some forms of Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity (Junge et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: The Munc13-1 C1 domain mediates diacylglycerol (DAG)- and phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release.
source: the C1 domain mediates diacylglycerol (DAG)- and phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release (Basu et al., 2007; Rhee et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2B domain acts as a Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent modulator of short-term plasticity.
source: the C2B domain acts as a Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent modulator of short-term plasticity (Shin et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: The MUN domain is a highly elongated module that is homologous to factors involved in tethering in diverse membrane compartments.
source: The MUN domain is a highly elongated module that is homologous to factors involved in tethering in diverse membrane compartments and is critical for opening syntaxin-1 (Basu et al., 2005; Ma et al., 2011; Pei et al., 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: The MUN domain is critical for opening syntaxin-1.
source: The MUN domain is a highly elongated module that is homologous to factors involved in tethering in diverse membrane compartments and is critical for opening syntaxin-1 (Basu et al., 2005; Ma et al., 2011; Pei et al., 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Multiple evidence suggests that the C2C domain is critical for Munc13 function.
source: Multiple evidence suggests that this domain is critical for Munc13 function (Liu et al., 2016; Madison et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2005), but its biochemical properties and mechanism of action are not well understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C domain is not predicted to bind Ca2+ because it lacks some of the canonical aspartate residues that typically bind Ca2+ in C2 domains.
source: Based on sequence alignments, the Munc13-1 C2C domain is not predicted to bind Ca2+ because it lacks some of the canonical aspartate residues that typically bind Ca2+ in C2 domains (Rizo and Südhof, 1998).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to known Ca2+-binding C2 domains.

claim: Reconstitution studies suggested that the C2C domain binds to membranes.
source: Reconstitution studies of synaptic vesicle fusion and vesicle clustering assays suggested that the C2C domain binds to membranes, leading to a model whereby the conserved Munc13-1 C-terminal region bridges the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes through respective interactions with the C2C domain and the C1-C2B region on opposite ends of the MUN domain (Liu et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous reconstitution studies.

claim: The C1 and C2B domains cooperate in binding to the plasma membrane through interactions with DAG and PIP2, respectively.
source: This model is consistent with the notion that the C1 and C2B domains cooperate in binding to the plasma membrane through interactions with DAG and PIP2, respectively (Basu et al., 2007; Rhee et al., 2002; Shin et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: A role for Munc13-1 in bridging membranes seems natural given the homology of the MUN domain with tethering factors.
source: and a role for Munc13-1 in bridging membranes seems natural given the homology of the MUN domain with tethering factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural homology.

claim: The physiological relevance of the membrane bridging model had not been investigated prior to this study.
source: However, no structure-function analysis of the C2C domain has been described, and the physiological relevance of the membrane bridging model has not been investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Lentiviral expression of full-length wild type Munc13-1 in Munc13-1/2 DKO neurons robustly rescues evoked release.
source: Lentiviral expression of full-length wild type (WT) Munc13-1 in neuronal autaptic cultures from Munc13-1/2 DKO mice robustly rescue evoked release, as observed previously (Liu et al., 2016), but almost no evoked release was observed when Munc13-1 lacking the C2C domain (Munc13-1 ΔC2C) was expressed (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Almost no evoked release was observed when Munc13-1 lacking the C2C domain (Munc13-1 ΔC2C) was expressed in Munc13-1/2 DKO neurons.
source: Lentiviral expression of full-length wild type (WT) Munc13-1 in neuronal autaptic cultures from Munc13-1/2 DKO mice robustly rescue evoked release, as observed previously (Liu et al., 2016), but almost no evoked release was observed when Munc13-1 lacking the C2C domain (Munc13-1 ΔC2C) was expressed (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Deletion of the C2C domain reduced the RRP strongly.
source: Deletion of the C2C domain also reduced the RRP strongly, although the impairment was not as severe as that observed for evoked release (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sucrose-induced release measurements in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The release probability of vesicles primed by Munc13-1 ΔC2C was decreased compared to WT Munc13-1.
source: As a result, the release probability of the few vesicles that were primed was decreased for the Munc13-1 ΔC2C rescue compared with the WT rescue (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of evoked release to RRP in Figure 1F.

claim: Synapses from neurons rescued with Munc13-1 ΔC2C exhibited facilitation upon repetitive stimulation, unlike those rescued with WT Munc13-1.
source: As expected from the decrease in vesicular release probability, we also found that synapses from neurons rescued with Munc13-1 ΔC2C exhibited facilitation upon repetitive stimulation, unlike those rescued with WT Munc13-1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by train stimulation data in Figure 1G.

claim: The C2C domain plays a critical role in synaptic exocytosis.
source: These results demonstrate that the Munc13-1 C2C domain plays a critical role in synaptic exocytosis, in agreement with previous results (Liu et al., 2016; Madison et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2005)
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the functional data and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The C2C domain is important for vesicle priming.
source: and show that this role is important for vesicle priming and also crucial for evoked neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is inferred from the RRP measurements showing reduced priming with C2C deletion.

claim: The C2C domain is crucial for evoked neurotransmitter release.
source: and show that this role is important for vesicle priming and also crucial for evoked neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the near-complete loss of evoked release with C2C deletion.

claim: A Munc13-1 MUNC2C fragment (including MUN and C2C domains) can be readily expressed in bacteria.
source: However, a longer fragment including the C2C domain and the preceding MUN domain (MUNC2C) can be readily expressed in bacteria (Liu et al., 2016), suggesting that the C2C domain requires packing against the MUN domain for proper folding.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from protein expression experiments.

claim: The C2C domain requires packing against the MUN domain for proper folding.
source: However, a longer fragment including the C2C domain and the preceding MUN domain (MUNC2C) can be readily expressed in bacteria (Liu et al., 2016), suggesting that the C2C domain requires packing against the MUN domain for proper folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to express isolated C2C domain but successful expression of MUNC2C.

claim: The C2C domain is structured within the MUNC2C fragment.
source: To confirm that the C2C domain is folded within the MUNC2C fragment, we compared 1H-13C heteronuclear multiple quantum coherence (HMQC) spectra of perdeuterated samples of the Munc13-1 MUN domain and MUNC2C fragment that were specifically 1H,13C-labeled at Ile, Leu and Val methyl groups (2H,13CH3-ILV-labeled). The spectrum of the MUNC2C fragment contains additional cross-peaks in well-resolved regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), showing that the C2C domain is structured.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectroscopy showing additional cross-peaks in MUNC2C compared to MUN alone.

claim: There are intramolecular interactions between the MUN and C2C domains.
source: In addition, the shifts observed in some of the cross-peaks of the MUN domain upon inclusion of the C2C domain support the notion that there are intramolecular interactions between the two domains.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR chemical shift changes observed when C2C is present.

claim: The C2C domain does not enhance the weak interaction of the MUN domain with syntaxin-1.
source: Hence, these results show that the two fragments bind very weakly to the syntaxin-1 (2–253) fragment and that the C2C domain does not enhance the weak interaction involving the MUN domain, as the presence of the C2C domain in MUNC2C did not increase the broadening.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR titration experiments showing similar weak binding for MUN and MUNC2C to syntaxin-1.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C domain binds weakly to membranes.
source: Hence, we hypothesized that the Munc13-1 C2C domain binds weakly to membranes and that such binding was not detectable in the co-floatation assays, but cooperativity between the C2C domains of two or more C1C2BMUNC2C molecules enables their liposome-liposome bridging activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the discrepancy between co-floatation and bridging assays.

claim: Cooperativity between the C2C domains of two or more C1C2BMUNC2C molecules enables their liposome-liposome bridging activity.
source: Hence, we hypothesized that the Munc13-1 C2C domain binds weakly to membranes and that such binding was not detectable in the co-floatation assays, but cooperativity between the C2C domains of two or more C1C2BMUNC2C molecules enables their liposome-liposome bridging activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the bridging activity.

claim: Membrane binding is the most common function of C2 domains.
source: Note that membrane binding is the most common function of C2 domains (Rizo and Südhof, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C2 domains, supported by citation.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C domain contains exposed basic and hydrophobic residues in its putative membrane-binding loops.
source: Indeed, models of the three-dimensional structure of the Munc13-1 C2C domain derived from its homology to C2 domains of known structure such as the synaptotagmin-1 C2B domain (Fernandez et al., 2001) and the RIM1 C2B domain (Guan et al., 2007) consistently predicted that the C2C domain contains exposed basic and hydrophobic residues in its putative membrane-binding loops, as well as a polybasic region on the side of the β-sandwich.
evidence: This is predicted from homology modeling based on known C2 domain structures.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C domain contains a polybasic region on the side of the β-sandwich.
source: Indeed, models of the three-dimensional structure of the Munc13-1 C2C domain derived from its homology to C2 domains of known structure such as the synaptotagmin-1 C2B domain (Fernandez et al., 2001) and the RIM1 C2B domain (Guan et al., 2007) consistently predicted that the C2C domain contains exposed basic and hydrophobic residues in its putative membrane-binding loops, as well as a polybasic region on the side of the β-sandwich.
evidence: This is predicted from homology modeling.

claim: WT GST-MUNC2C efficiently bound to rho-liposomes.
source: These results show that WT GST-MUNC2C efficiently bound to the rho-liposomes, while there was no detectable binding for the R1598E/F1658E GST-MUNC2C mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST-pulldown assays showing retention of liposomes by WT but not mutant protein (Figure 2C,D).

claim: The R1598E/F1658E mutation abolishes binding of MUNC2C to membranes.
source: These results show that WT GST-MUNC2C efficiently bound to the rho-liposomes, while there was no detectable binding for the R1598E/F1658E GST-MUNC2C mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST-pulldown assays (Figure 2C,D).

claim: The Munc13-1 MUNC2C fragment binds to membranes.
source: Overall, these results show that the Munc13-1 MUNC2C fragment indeed binds to membranes, and that this activity is abolished by the R1598E/F1658E mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST-pulldown assays.

claim: The MUN domain has a highly elongated structure.
source: The MUN domain has a highly elongated structure (Xu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015), with the C1-C2B region and the C2C domain attached at opposite ends.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The C1-C2B region and the C2C domain are attached at opposite ends of the MUN domain.
source: The MUN domain has a highly elongated structure (Xu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015), with the C1-C2B region and the C2C domain attached at opposite ends.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the MUN domain.

claim: Many instances were observed where two liposomes were bridged by highly elongated densities in cryo-ET images.
source: Indeed, we observed many instances where two liposomes were bridged by highly elongated densities (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is directly visualized in cryo-ET images in Figure 3A-E.

claim: The average length of highly elongated densities bridging liposomes was 22 nm.
source: Measurements made for 70 of these highly elongated densities yielded an average length of 22 nm, consistent with the approximate length that can be predicted for C1C2BMUNC2C based on the crystal structure of the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUN fragment (ca. 20 nm long [Xu et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is measured from cryo-ET images and compared to predicted length from crystal structure.

claim: The elongated densities bridging liposomes can be attributed unambiguously to the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment.
source: Because the three-dimensional structures of all the other proteins included in the samples are known and none of them has such an elongated shape (Rizo, 2018), these densities can be attributed unambiguously to the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment.
evidence: This is inferred from the unique elongated shape matching C1C2BMUNC2C and not other proteins in the sample.

claim: Liposomes generally formed clusters where each liposome pair was bridged by at least one, and often more, C1C2BMUNC2C molecules.
source: We note that liposomes generally formed clusters where each liposome pair was bridged by at least one, and often more, C1C2BMUNC2C molecules that likely cooperate in clustering.
evidence: This is observed in cryo-ET images.

claim: Super-resolution imaging revealed the formation of supramolecular assemblies by multiple Munc13-1 molecules at presynaptic release sites.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that super-resolution imaging revealed the formation of supramolecular assemblies by multiple Munc13-1 molecules at presynaptic release sites (Sakamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a super-resolution imaging study.

claim: Among 123 molecules of WT C1C2BMUNC2C identified in cryo-ET, 78 were bridging two liposomes and 45 were bound to a single liposome.
source: In contrast, among 123 molecules of WT C1C2BMUNC2C that we identified, 78 were bridging two liposomes and 45 were bound to a single liposome (25 among these 45 likely did not bridge liposomes due to steric hindrance caused by other C1C2BMUNC2C molecules at the liposome-liposome interface).
evidence: This is quantified from cryo-ET images.

claim: All 42 identified C1C2BMUNC2C R1598E/F1658E mutant molecules were bound to a single liposome.
source: Nevertheless, we were able to identify 42 C1C2BMUNC2C R1598E/F1658E mutant molecules, and all of them were bound to a single liposome.
evidence: This is quantified from cryo-ET images.

claim: The R1598E/F1658E mutation completely abrogates liposome clustering by C1C2BMUNC2C.
source: These results are consistent with dynamic light scattering (DLS) data showing complete abrogation of liposome clustering by the R1598E/F1658E mutation (see below)
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 5.

claim: Binding of the C2C domain to lipids is key for the membrane-bridging activity of C1C2BMUNC2C.
source: and strongly support the notion that binding of the C2C domain to lipids is key for the membrane-bridging activity of C1C2BMUNC2C.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-ET and DLS data showing loss of bridging with C2C mutations.

claim: C1C2BMUNC2C robustly clusters SV- and PM-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+.
source: The data showed that C1C2BMUNC2C robustly clusters SV- and PM-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+ and that Ca2+ does not substantially increase this activity (Figure 4A), as observed previously with V- and T-liposome mixtures (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 4A.

claim: Ca2+ does not substantially increase the clustering activity of C1C2BMUNC2C.
source: The data showed that C1C2BMUNC2C robustly clusters SV- and PM-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+ and that Ca2+ does not substantially increase this activity (Figure 4A), as observed previously with V- and T-liposome mixtures (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 4A.

claim: Membrane bridging by C1C2BMUNC2C involves direct interactions with the two apposed membranes.
source: These results demonstrate that membrane bridging involves direct interactions of C1C2BMUNC2C with the two apposed membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by clustering of protein-free liposomes by C1C2BMUNC2C.

claim: The C1C2BMUN fragment ending at residue 1531 was able to cluster liposomes.
source: The importance of the C2C domain for bridging might be questioned because the C1C2BMUN fragment that we used in previous studies was also able to cluster liposomes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a previous observation that needs to be reconciled with the current findings.

claim: The sequence spanning residues 1517 to 1531 is not part of the folded structure of the MUN domain.
source: However, in this previous study , we noted that the C1C2BMUN fragment used ended at residue 1531 and that the sequence spanning residues 1517 to 1531 is not part of the folded structure of the MUN domain.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the MUN domain.

claim: The sequence spanning residues 1517 to 1531 is highly hydrophobic and likely mediates non-specific binding to membranes.
source: This sequence is highly hydrophobic and is probably folded in the C1C2BMUNC2C fragment, but is not observable in the structure of C1C2BMUN (Xu et al., 2017). Hence, this sequence is exposed and likely mediates non-specific binding to membranes, which explains the ability of the C1C2BMUN fragment to cluster liposomes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the hydrophobic nature of the sequence and its exposure in C1C2BMUN1531.

claim: The C1C2BMUN1516 fragment exhibited no clustering ability.
source: DLS assays showed that, in contrast to C1C2BMUNC2C, the C1C2BMUN1516 fragment exhibited no clustering ability (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 4A.

claim: The C2C domain is crucial for the membrane bridging activity of the Munc13-1 C-terminal region.
source: These results strongly support the notion that the C2C domain is indeed crucial for the membrane bridging activity of the Munc13-1 C-terminal region.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of C1C2BMUNC2C and C1C2BMUN1516 clustering activities.

claim: Bacterially expressed C1C2BMUNC2C and C1C2BMUN1516 fragments have analogous ability, or lack thereof, to cluster SV- and PM-liposomes as the corresponding fragments expressed in Sf9 cells.
source: DLS experiments showed that the bacterially expressed C1C2BMUNC2C and C1C2BMUN1516 fragments have analogous ability, or lack thereof, to cluster SV- and PM-liposomes as the corresponding fragments expressed in Sf9 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data comparing bacterial and Sf9-expressed proteins.

claim: C1C2BMUNC2C fragments expressed in Sf9 insect cells and E. coli exhibited comparable activities in supporting fusion between reconstituted V- and T-liposomes.
source: The C1C2BMUNC2C fragments expressed in Sf9 insect cells and E. coli exhibited comparable activities, with slow lipid and content mixing in the absence of Ca2+ and fast fusion upon Ca2+ influx (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays comparing bacterial and Sf9-expressed proteins.

claim: The C1C2BMUN1516 fragments expressed in Sf9 insect cells and E. coli were both inactive in supporting liposome fusion.
source: In contrast, the C1C2BMUN1516 fragments expressed in Sf9 insect cells and E. coli were both inactive, which correlates with the vesicle clustering results and shows the critical importance of the C2C domain for Munc13-1 to support fusion in these assays.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays showing no activity for C1C2BMUN1516.

claim: The C2C domain is critical for Munc13-1 to support fusion in reconstituted assays.
source: In contrast, the C1C2BMUN1516 fragments expressed in Sf9 insect cells and E. coli were both inactive, which correlates with the vesicle clustering results and shows the critical importance of the C2C domain for Munc13-1 to support fusion in these assays.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of fusion activities of C1C2BMUNC2C and C1C2BMUN1516.

claim: The C1C2BMUN1516 fragments are properly folded and retain the ability of the C1-C2B region to bind to liposomes containing DAG and PIP2.
source: We also note that the C1C2BMUN1516 fragments made in Sf9 insect cells and in bacteria exhibited the expected chromatographic behavior in gel filtration, with elution volume a little larger than the C1C2BMUNC2C fragments (16.5 versus 16.2 ml in a Superdex S200 10/300 GL column), and a similar ability to bind to PM-liposomes in co-sedimentation assays as C1C2BMUNC2C fragments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). These results indicate that the C1C2BMUN1516 fragments are properly folded and retain the ability of the C1-C2B region to bind to liposomes containing DAG and PIP2, but cannot bridge these liposomes to SV-liposomes because they lack the C2C domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel filtration and co-sedimentation assays.

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation partially disrupts the clustering activity of C1C2BMUNC2C.
source: DLS assays that monitored clustering between SV- and PM-liposomes revealed that the K1613A/K1616A mutation partially disrupts the clustering activity of C1C2BMUNC2C (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 5.

claim: The single R1598E and F1658E mutations disrupted vesicle clustering strongly.
source: The single R1598E and F1658E mutations disrupted vesicle clustering strongly, although the R1598E mutant appeared to retain a slight clustering ability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 5.

claim: Clustering was completely abolished by the R1598E/F1658E mutation.
source: Clustering was completely abolished by the R1598E/F1658E mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DLS data in Figure 5.

claim: The C2C domain loops are critical for membrane bridging by the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment.
source: These results demonstrate the critical importance of the C2C domain loops for membrane bridging by the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment, and show that the C2C domain polybasic region also contributes to this activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the effects of mutations in the loops on clustering.

claim: The C2C domain polybasic region contributes to membrane bridging activity.
source: These results demonstrate the critical importance of the C2C domain loops for membrane bridging by the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment, and show that the C2C domain polybasic region also contributes to this activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the partial effect of K1613A/K1616A mutation on clustering.

claim: F1658 is a key residue that inserts into the bilayer to mediate binding.
source: Conversely, the effects of the mutations can be readily rationalized by the accumulated knowledge on membrane binding to C2 domains, which predicts that F1658 is a key residue that inserts into the bilayer to mediate binding (Chapman and Davis, 1998; Rhee et al., 2005), while the polybasic region including K1613 and K1616 is expected to contribute to membrane binding but to a more moderate extent (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of C2 domain membrane binding mechanisms and the strong effect of F1658E mutation.

claim: The polybasic region including K1613 and K1616 is expected to contribute to membrane binding but to a more moderate extent.
source: Conversely, the effects of the mutations can be readily rationalized by the accumulated knowledge on membrane binding to C2 domains, which predicts that F1658 is a key residue that inserts into the bilayer to mediate binding (Chapman and Davis, 1998; Rhee et al., 2005), while the polybasic region including K1613 and K1616 is expected to contribute to membrane binding but to a more moderate extent (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of C2 domain membrane binding and the moderate effect of K1613A/K1616A mutation.

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation considerably impaired fusion at 0.1 μM concentration.
source: At this concentration, the K1613A/K1616A mutation considerably impaired fusion, whereas the R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations completely abolished fusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays in Figure 6A.

claim: The R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations completely abolished fusion at 0.1 μM concentration.
source: At this concentration, the K1613A/K1616A mutation considerably impaired fusion, whereas the R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations completely abolished fusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays in Figure 6A.

claim: The F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations almost completely abolish the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion.
source: Overall, these results show that the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations almost completely abolish the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion, whereas the R1598E mutation causes a strong disruption, and the K1613A/K1616A mutation induces only a moderate impairment, mirroring the liposome clustering data.
evidence: This is concluded from fusion assays at various concentrations (Figure 6).

claim: The R1598E mutation causes a strong disruption of the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion.
source: Overall, these results show that the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations almost completely abolish the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion, whereas the R1598E mutation causes a strong disruption, and the K1613A/K1616A mutation induces only a moderate impairment, mirroring the liposome clustering data.
evidence: This is concluded from fusion assays at various concentrations (Figure 6).

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation induces only a moderate impairment of the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion.
source: Overall, these results show that the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations almost completely abolish the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion, whereas the R1598E mutation causes a strong disruption, and the K1613A/K1616A mutation induces only a moderate impairment, mirroring the liposome clustering data.
evidence: This is concluded from fusion assays at various concentrations (Figure 6).

claim: The effects of mutations on fusion mirror the liposome clustering data.
source: Overall, these results show that the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations almost completely abolish the ability of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C to support membrane fusion, whereas the R1598E mutation causes a strong disruption, and the K1613A/K1616A mutation induces only a moderate impairment, mirroring the liposome clustering data.
evidence: This is a comparison of the relative effects of mutations on clustering and fusion.

claim: The R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations severely impaired spontaneous, evoked and sucrose-induced release in neurons.
source: The R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations severely impaired spontaneous, evoked and sucrose-induced release, and the effects were particularly strong for evoked release, which was almost abolished by the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7.

claim: Evoked release was almost abolished by the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations.
source: The R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations severely impaired spontaneous, evoked and sucrose-induced release, and the effects were particularly strong for evoked release, which was almost abolished by the F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7E.

claim: The R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutations led to decreases in the vesicular release probability.
source: As a consequence of the stronger impairment of evoked release compared to sucrose-induced release, the three mutations led to decreases in the vesicular release probability (Figure 7G), as observed for the Munc13-1 ΔC2C mutant (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of evoked release to RRP in Figure 7G.

claim: The paired-pulse ratios measured for the R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutants were larger than that observed for WT Munc13-1.
source: Correspondingly, the paired-pulsed ratios measured for the three mutants were larger than that observed for WT Munc13-1 (Figure 7H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired-pulse experiments in Figure 7H.

claim: All the R1598E, F1658E and R1598E/F1658E mutant rescues exhibited facilitation upon repetitive stimulation, in contrast to the slight depression observed in the WT rescue.
source: and all the mutant rescues exhibited facilitation upon repetitive stimulation, in contrast to the slight depression observed in the WT rescue (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by train stimulation data in Figure 7I.

claim: The WT and mutant Munc13-1 proteins all exhibited presynaptic localization and were expressed at comparable levels.
source: The WT and mutant Munc13-1 proteins all exhibited presynaptic localization and were expressed at comparable levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), showing that the differences in electrophysiological parameters do not arise from mislocalization or aberrant overexpression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunocytochemistry in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation did not impair spontaneous release.
source: This mutation did not impair spontaneous release but led to a moderate decrease in evoked release, and also appeared to decrease the RRP but the difference to WT was not statistically significant (Figure 8A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 8D.

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation led to a moderate decrease in evoked release.
source: This mutation did not impair spontaneous release but led to a moderate decrease in evoked release, and also appeared to decrease the RRP but the difference to WT was not statistically significant (Figure 8A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 8E.

claim: The ability of mutations in the Munc13-1 C2C domain to impair liposome clustering and fusion in vitro correlates well with the functional effects of these mutations on synaptic vesicle priming and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in neurons.
source: These results show that the ability of these various mutations in the Munc13-1 C2C domain to impair liposome clustering and fusion in vitro correlates well with the functional effects of these mutations on synaptic vesicle priming and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release in neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing in vitro and in vivo effects of mutations.

claim: Overexpression of the four Munc13-1 mutants in WT neurons did not yield significant differences compared to overexpression of WT Munc13-1.
source: We also tested whether overexpression of the four Munc13-1 mutants in neurons from WT mice yielded differences in spontaneous, evoked and sucrose-induced release with respect to overexpression of WT Munc13-1, but we did not observe any significant differences that would suggest a dominant negative effect of the mutant fragments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Synaptic vesicle docking is strongly impaired in Munc13-1/2 DKO neurons.
source: Previous studies that used high-pressure freezing/freeze substitution of organotypic hippocampal slice cultures and electron tomography showed that synaptic vesicle docking is strongly impaired in Munc13-1/2 DKO neurons, defining docking as vesicles that appear to be in direct contact with presynaptic active zone membranes (Imig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous electron microscopy study.

claim: Significant defects in docking were observed for all Munc13-1 mutants tested.
source: Significant defects in docking were observed for all Munc13-1 mutants, with the R1598E/F1658E mutation having the strongest effect and the K1613A/K161A mutation the mildest (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9A,B.

claim: The R1598E/F1658E mutation had the strongest effect on docking among the mutants tested.
source: Significant defects in docking were observed for all Munc13-1 mutants, with the R1598E/F1658E mutation having the strongest effect and the K1613A/K161A mutation the mildest (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9B.

claim: The K1613A/K1616A mutation had the mildest effect on docking among the mutants tested.
source: Significant defects in docking were observed for all Munc13-1 mutants, with the R1598E/F1658E mutation having the strongest effect and the K1613A/K161A mutation the mildest (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9B.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the normalized number of docked synaptic vesicles and the RRP charge for WT and mutant Munc13-1 fragments.
source: A plot of the normalized number of docked synaptic vesicles observed for the WT and mutant Munc13-1 fragments against the RRP charge shows a strong correlation (Figure 9C), supporting the notion that docking and priming are closely related.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation plot in Figure 9C.

claim: Docking and priming are closely related.
source: A plot of the normalized number of docked synaptic vesicles observed for the WT and mutant Munc13-1 fragments against the RRP charge shows a strong correlation (Figure 9C), supporting the notion that docking and priming are closely related.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between docking and RRP.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C domain is critical for synaptic vesicle docking, priming and Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate the critical importance of the Munc13-1 C2C domain for synaptic vesicle docking, priming and, particularly, Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined electrophysiology and electron microscopy data.

claim: The correlation between the physiological effects caused by the mutations and those caused on liposome clustering and membrane fusion provides strong evidence that the ability of Munc13-1 to bridge membranes is crucial for neurotransmitter release.
source: Moreover, the correlation between the physiological effects caused by the mutations and those caused on liposome clustering and membrane fusion provide strong evidence that the ability of Munc13-1 to bridge membranes is crucial for neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the parallel effects of mutations in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Munc18-1 and Munc13s orchestrate SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner.
source: Great advances have been recently made in understanding the mechanism of neurotransmitter release, including the fundamental concept that Munc18-1 and Munc13s orchestrate SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner (Ma et al., 2013) that explains at least in part the total abrogation of neurotransmitter release observed in the absence of Munc18-1 or Munc13s (Richmond et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Verhage et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The total abrogation of neurotransmitter release observed in the absence of Munc18-1 or Munc13s is explained at least in part by their role in orchestrating SNARE complex assembly.
source: Great advances have been recently made in understanding the mechanism of neurotransmitter release, including the fundamental concept that Munc18-1 and Munc13s orchestrate SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner (Ma et al., 2013) that explains at least in part the total abrogation of neurotransmitter release observed in the absence of Munc18-1 or Munc13s (Richmond et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Verhage et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the molecular mechanism to the phenotype.

claim: The actual pathway of SNARE complex assembly is still under intense investigation.
source: Nevertheless, the actual pathway of SNARE complex assembly is still under intense investigation.
evidence: This is stated as current state of the field.

claim: The critical role of Munc13s in SNARE complex assembly has generally been associated with the activity of the MUN domain in facilitating opening of syntaxin-1.
source: The critical role of Munc13s in this process has generally been associated to the activity of its MUN domain in facilitating opening of syntaxin-1 (Ma et al., 2011; Richmond et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015), but this activity alone does not account for the functional importance of the Munc13 C2C domain, which was suggested by diverse studies (Liu et al., 2016; Madison et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2005) and is further supported here (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The activity of the MUN domain in facilitating opening of syntaxin-1 alone does not account for the functional importance of the Munc13 C2C domain.
source: The critical role of Munc13s in this process has generally been associated to the activity of its MUN domain in facilitating opening of syntaxin-1 (Ma et al., 2011; Richmond et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015), but this activity alone does not account for the functional importance of the Munc13 C2C domain, which was suggested by diverse studies (Liu et al., 2016; Madison et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2005) and is further supported here (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that C2C domain is critical for function beyond syntaxin-1 opening.

claim: The highly conserved C-terminal region of Munc13-1 can bridge two membranes.
source: Here, we provide compelling evidence that the highly conserved C-terminal region of Munc13-1 can indeed bridge two membranes, that the C2C domain is critical for this activity, and that membrane bridging is a key aspect of the function of Munc13-1 in synaptic vesicle docking, priming and fusion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Membrane bridging is a key aspect of the function of Munc13-1 in synaptic vesicle docking, priming and fusion.
source: Here, we provide compelling evidence that the highly conserved C-terminal region of Munc13-1 can indeed bridge two membranes, that the C2C domain is critical for this activity, and that membrane bridging is a key aspect of the function of Munc13-1 in synaptic vesicle docking, priming and fusion.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the correlation between bridging and function.

claim: A single point mutation in the 200 kDa Munc13-1 protein abolishes neurotransmitter release almost completely.
source: The importance of this bridging function is emphasized by the finding that a single point mutation in this 200 kDa protein abolishes neurotransmitter release almost completely.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the F1658E mutation data.

claim: Membrane bridging may constitute the primary function of Munc13s.
source: This dramatic result suggests that membrane bridging may in fact constitute the primary function of Munc13s, although this notion does not diminish the importance of their role in opening syntaxin-1 because the two activities are likely coupled.
evidence: This is speculated based on the dramatic effect of disrupting bridging.

claim: The membrane bridging and syntaxin-1 opening activities of Munc13s are likely coupled.
source: This dramatic result suggests that membrane bridging may in fact constitute the primary function of Munc13s, although this notion does not diminish the importance of their role in opening syntaxin-1 because the two activities are likely coupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional relationship between bridging and SNARE assembly.

claim: Formation of SNARE complexes is hindered by the closed conformation of syntaxin-1.
source: Formation of SNARE complexes is hindered not only by the closed conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999) but also by the furled conformation of a Munc18-1 loop that prevents synaptobrevin binding and hence hinders the SNARE complex templating function of Munc18-1 (Sitarska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Formation of SNARE complexes is hindered by the furled conformation of a Munc18-1 loop that prevents synaptobrevin binding.
source: Formation of SNARE complexes is hindered not only by the closed conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999) but also by the furled conformation of a Munc18-1 loop that prevents synaptobrevin binding and hence hinders the SNARE complex templating function of Munc18-1 (Sitarska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study.

claim: The bridge between the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes provided by Munc13-1 is expected to dramatically increase the number of productive encounters between synaptobrevin and the syntaxin-1-Munc18-1 complex.
source: The bridge between the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes provided by Munc13-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) is expected to dramatically increase the number of productive encounters between synaptobrevin and the syntaxin-1-Munc18-1 complex to initiate SNARE complex formation (Xu et al., 2017), further facilitated by the activity of the Munc13-1 MUN domain in opening syntaxin-1 (Ma et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about how bridging facilitates SNARE assembly.

claim: A membrane bridging function for Munc13s is not surprising given the homology of their MUN domain with tethering factors from different membrane compartments.
source: Note also that a membrane bridging function for Munc13s is not surprising given the homology of their MUN domain with tethering factors from different membrane compartments (Pei et al., 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from structural homology.

claim: Tethering factors homologous to the MUN domain normally do not contain C1 or C2 domains.
source: However, these factors normally do not contain C1 or C2 domains.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of Munc13s compared to other tethering factors.

claim: The incorporation of membrane-binding C1 and C2 domains at both ends of the Munc13 MUN domain may have occurred during evolution to provide opportunities for regulation of membrane-bridging activity.
source: The incorporation of membrane-binding C1 and C2 domains at both ends of the Munc13 MUN domain may have occurred during evolution to provide opportunities for regulation of this membrane-bridging activity, as exquisite regulation is a hallmark of neurotransmitter release and Munc13-1 acts as a master regulator of this process (Rizo, 2018).
evidence: This is an evolutionary speculation about the function of the C1 and C2 domains.

claim: Exquisite regulation is a hallmark of neurotransmitter release.
source: The incorporation of membrane-binding C1 and C2 domains at both ends of the Munc13 MUN domain may have occurred during evolution to provide opportunities for regulation of this membrane-bridging activity, as exquisite regulation is a hallmark of neurotransmitter release and Munc13-1 acts as a master regulator of this process (Rizo, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurotransmitter release.

claim: Munc13-1 acts as a master regulator of neurotransmitter release.
source: The incorporation of membrane-binding C1 and C2 domains at both ends of the Munc13 MUN domain may have occurred during evolution to provide opportunities for regulation of this membrane-bridging activity, as exquisite regulation is a hallmark of neurotransmitter release and Munc13-1 acts as a master regulator of this process (Rizo, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: The C2C domain is not known to be involved in plasticity.
source: The C2C domain is not known to be involved in plasticity, but it is tempting to speculate that as yet unidentified mechanisms (e.g. phosphorylation) may modulate C2C domain activity to regulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge and a speculation about future possibilities.

claim: As yet unidentified mechanisms (e.g. phosphorylation) may modulate C2C domain activity to regulate neurotransmitter release.
source: The C2C domain is not known to be involved in plasticity, but it is tempting to speculate that as yet unidentified mechanisms (e.g. phosphorylation) may modulate C2C domain activity to regulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The membrane-bridging activity of the Munc13 C-terminal region is important for more than one of the steps that lead to release.
source: The finding that the C2C deletion and the mutations in the Munc13-1 C2C domain described here impair synaptic vesicle docking, priming and release (Figures 1 and 7–9), in correlation with the impairments they cause in liposome clustering and fusion in vitro (Figures 4–6), suggests that the membrane-bridging activity of the Munc13 C-terminal region is important for more than one of the steps that lead to release.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple effects of C2C mutations on different steps of release.

claim: The role of Munc13-1 in docking-priming is not unexpected, as SNARE complex assembly is believed to be necessary for vesicle docking.
source: The role in docking-priming is not unexpected, as SNARE complex assembly is believed to be necessary for vesicle docking using the definition that has become widely used recently and we adopt here, that is contact between the vesicle and plasma membranes (Imig et al., 2014) (note that, with this definition, docking and priming may constitute the same event, although this equivalence is not fully established [Rizo, 2018]).
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between SNARE assembly and docking.

claim: With the current definition of docking, docking and priming may constitute the same event, although this equivalence is not fully established.
source: The role in docking-priming is not unexpected, as SNARE complex assembly is believed to be necessary for vesicle docking using the definition that has become widely used recently and we adopt here, that is contact between the vesicle and plasma membranes (Imig et al., 2014) (note that, with this definition, docking and priming may constitute the same event, although this equivalence is not fully established [Rizo, 2018]).
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: The phenotypic spectra in Munc13-1 mutants and in syntaxin-1 titration experiments are highly similar.
source: Moreover, the phenotypic spectra in Munc13-1 mutants and in syntaxin-1 titration experiments are highly similar (Arancillo et al., 2013), supporting the hypothesis that Munc13-1 membrane bridging and SNARE complex assembly are tightly linked.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Munc13-1 membrane bridging and SNARE complex assembly are tightly linked.
source: Moreover, the phenotypic spectra in Munc13-1 mutants and in syntaxin-1 titration experiments are highly similar (Arancillo et al., 2013), supporting the hypothesis that Munc13-1 membrane bridging and SNARE complex assembly are tightly linked.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes.

claim: In vivo, synaptic vesicles are believed to be tethered to the active zone through other mechanisms, for instance through RIM-Rab3 interactions.
source: Note however that, in vivo, synaptic vesicles are believed to be tethered to the active zone through other mechanisms, for instance through RIM-Rab3 interactions, and Munc13 function may be partially redundant with that of CAPS, which contains a MUN domain and membrane-binding domains and also supports SNARE-dependent fusion in reconstitution assays (James et al., 2009) (reviewed in Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vesicle tethering mechanisms.

claim: Munc13 function may be partially redundant with that of CAPS.
source: Note however that, in vivo, synaptic vesicles are believed to be tethered to the active zone through other mechanisms, for instance through RIM-Rab3 interactions, and Munc13 function may be partially redundant with that of CAPS, which contains a MUN domain and membrane-binding domains and also supports SNARE-dependent fusion in reconstitution assays (James et al., 2009) (reviewed in Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar domain architecture and function of CAPS.

claim: CAPS contains a MUN domain and membrane-binding domains and supports SNARE-dependent fusion in reconstitution assays.
source: Note however that, in vivo, synaptic vesicles are believed to be tethered to the active zone through other mechanisms, for instance through RIM-Rab3 interactions, and Munc13 function may be partially redundant with that of CAPS, which contains a MUN domain and membrane-binding domains and also supports SNARE-dependent fusion in reconstitution assays (James et al., 2009) (reviewed in Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CAPS.

claim: Redundancy with other tethering mechanisms may explain why the effects of the Munc13-1 C2C domain mutations on liposome clustering and fusion in vitro are stronger than those observed in vesicle docking and priming in neurons.
source: Such redundancy may explain the finding that the effects of the Munc13-1 C2C domain mutations on the liposome clustering and fusion assays in vitro (Figures 5–6) are stronger than those observed in vesicle docking and priming in neurons (Figures 7–9).
evidence: This is inferred as an explanation for the difference between in vitro and in vivo effects.

claim: The Munc13-1 C2C mutations disrupt Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release at least as much as they impair docking and priming.
source: Interestingly, the Munc13-1 C2C mutations also disrupt Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release at least as much as they impair docking and priming.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the effects on evoked release versus RRP.

claim: The membrane bridging activity of Munc13-1 is as important for release itself as for vesicle docking-priming.
source: These observations suggest that the membrane bridging activity of Munc13-1 is as important for release itself as for vesicle docking-priming.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable effects of mutations on release and docking-priming.

claim: It is plausible that Munc13-1 still bridges the primed vesicles to the plasma membrane, forming part of the macromolecular assembly that triggers fusion.
source: It is also plausible that the C2C domain mutations impair only SNARE complex assembly and a lower number of assembled SNARE complexes results in a stronger impairment of Ca2+-triggered fusion than of sucrose-induced release or the number of docked vesicles. Both explanations are not mutually exclusive, but the notion that Munc13-1 still bridges the primed vesicles to the plasma membrane, forming part of the macromolecular assembly that triggers fusion, is attractive because it can explain the multiple and distinct effects of Munc13-1 mutations on vesicular release probability (Figures 1F and 7G, and Basu et al., 2007; Junge et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is proposed as a plausible model to explain the data.

claim: Phorbol ester stimulation of Munc13-1 C1 domains acutely increases release probability without changing the number of docked and primed vesicles.
source: In particular, the finding that phorbol ester stimulation of Munc13-1 C1 domains acutely increases release probability without changing the number of docked and primed vesicles (Basu et al., 2007; Camacho et al., 2017) strongly suggests that modulation of the Munc13 bridging function may directly regulate the efficiency of the vesicle fusion reaction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Modulation of the Munc13 bridging function may directly regulate the efficiency of the vesicle fusion reaction.
source: In particular, the finding that phorbol ester stimulation of Munc13-1 C1 domains acutely increases release probability without changing the number of docked and primed vesicles (Basu et al., 2007; Camacho et al., 2017) strongly suggests that modulation of the Munc13 bridging function may directly regulate the efficiency of the vesicle fusion reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the phorbol ester effects on release probability.

claim: The model that Munc13-1 bridges primed vesicles is consistent with super-resolution imaging data showing that Munc13-1 and Unc13 form supramolecular assemblies at release sites.
source: This model is also consistent with recent super-resolution imaging data showing that mammalian Munc13-1 and invertebrate Unc13 form supramolecular assemblies that appear to define the sites for neurotransmitter release in the presynaptic terminal (Reddy-Alla et al., 2017; Sakamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to super-resolution imaging studies.

claim: The Munc13-1 C-terminal region can likely bridge two membranes in at least two different orientations.
source: It is worth noting that the Munc13-1 C-terminal region can likely bridge two membranes in at least two different orientations that can favor SNARE complex formation and/or fusion to different extents, or can also inhibit these events, thus acting as a 'gatekeeper' of release.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: Munc13-1 can act as a 'gatekeeper' of release by bridging membranes in different orientations.
source: It is worth noting that the Munc13-1 C-terminal region can likely bridge two membranes in at least two different orientations that can favor SNARE complex formation and/or fusion to different extents, or can also inhibit these events, thus acting as a 'gatekeeper' of release.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed to explain regulation of release.

claim: The C1 and C2B domains have their respective DAG- and Ca2+-PIP2-binding sites next to each other and can cooperate in binding to the plasma membrane in a defined, slanted orientation.
source: This notion emerged from the finding that the C1 and C2B domains have their respective DAG- and Ca2+-PIP2-binding sites next to each other and can thus cooperate in binding to the plasma membrane in a defined, slanted orientation, but these domains also form a polybasic region that can bind to membranes in a different orientation, more perpendicular to the membrane (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural and functional study.

claim: The C1 and C2B domains form a polybasic region that can bind to membranes in a different orientation, more perpendicular to the membrane.
source: This notion emerged from the finding that the C1 and C2B domains have their respective DAG- and Ca2+-PIP2-binding sites next to each other and can thus cooperate in binding to the plasma membrane in a defined, slanted orientation, but these domains also form a polybasic region that can bind to membranes in a different orientation, more perpendicular to the membrane (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural and functional study.

claim: The model of different membrane-binding orientations provides a basis to understand DAG- and Ca2+-dependent presynaptic plasticity that depends on Munc13.
source: This model provides a basis to understand DAG- and Ca2+-dependent presynaptic plasticity that depends on Munc13, and explains the observation that membrane fusion does not occur or is very slow in the absence of Ca2+ even though Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes under these conditions (Figure 3), whereas fusion is fast upon Ca2+-binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016) (e.g. Figures 4B and 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation connecting structure to function.

claim: Membrane fusion does not occur or is very slow in the absence of Ca2+ even though Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes under these conditions.
source: This model provides a basis to understand DAG- and Ca2+-dependent presynaptic plasticity that depends on Munc13, and explains the observation that membrane fusion does not occur or is very slow in the absence of Ca2+ even though Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes under these conditions (Figure 3), whereas fusion is fast upon Ca2+-binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016) (e.g. Figures 4B and 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays and cryo-ET data.

claim: Fusion is fast upon Ca2+-binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain.
source: This model provides a basis to understand DAG- and Ca2+-dependent presynaptic plasticity that depends on Munc13, and explains the observation that membrane fusion does not occur or is very slow in the absence of Ca2+ even though Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C bridges membranes under these conditions (Figure 3), whereas fusion is fast upon Ca2+-binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016) (e.g. Figures 4B and 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays showing rapid fusion upon Ca2+ addition.

claim: Mutagenesis studies of C. elegans Unc13 support the idea that Unc13 can exist in two states, one that inhibits release and another that activates release and is favored by Ca2+-binding to the C2B domain.
source: Mutagenesis studies of C. elegans Unc13 support the idea that Unc13 can exist in two states, one that inhibits release and another that activates release and is favored by Ca2+-binding to the C2B domain (Michelassi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a mutagenesis study in C. elegans.

claim: Cryo-ET images show that Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C can bridge two membranes in a range of orientations in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Our cryo-ET images, which were acquired in the absence of Ca2+, show that Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C can bridge two membranes in a range of orientations, some of which would prevent the membranes from coming closer while others could favor initiation of SNARE complex assembly.
evidence: This is observed in cryo-ET images (Figure 3).

claim: Ca2+, DAG and PIP2 favor more slanted orientations of Munc13-1 that can facilitate SNARE complex formation more efficiently and/or membrane fusion.
source: We previously proposed that Ca2+, DAG and PIP2 favor more slanted orientations that can facilitate SNARE complex formation more efficiently and/or membrane fusion (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a previously proposed model, supported by citation.
